hook: Two massive planets will converge within 1 degree in November 2026.

sections.voiceover: Two massive planets will converge within 1 degree in November 2026.
sections.visual_cue: Cinematic wide rendering of Jupiter and Mars closing distance against a dark starry void.
sections.sfx_cue: Deep sub-bass rumble swell with subtle cosmic shimmer.

sections.voiceover: On November 16, 2026, Jupiter and Mars align in the morning sky. WhatTheStar reports they pass 1.2 degrees apart. Where will observers spot bright Jupiter near star Regulus?
sections.visual_cue: Telescopic simulation showing Mars and Jupiter positioning near the bright star Regulus at dawn.
sections.sfx_cue: Soft radio telemetry bleeps and calm ambient synth pad.
b_roll: Astronomical observatory dome opening at dawn
Star chart map showing Leo constellation

sections.voiceover: However, EarthSky notes they'll shine in the east with the star Regulus positioned below them.
sections.visual_cue: Split view of red disk of Mars alongside radiant white disc of Jupiter in predawn sky.

sections.voiceover: BBC Sky at Night Magazine confirms they reach 1 degree separation. Jupiter shines at magnitude -2.1 beside red Mars. Hunt notes Chicago observers see them before sunrise.
sections.visual_cue: Detailed orbital diagram showing line of sight from Chicago through atmosphere to Jupiter and Mars.
sections.sfx_cue: Resonant metallic chime with rising synth orchestra.
b_roll: Astronomical chart demonstrating planetary magnitude scale

sections.voiceover: The planetary alignment reaches 1.2 degrees separation on November 16.
sections.visual_cue: Wide cinematic camera pullback from aligned planets fading into cosmic background.
sections.sfx_cue: Sustaining deep ambient note dying out.
b_roll: Wide deep space starfield panning shot
